sections.section_title: Atypical Neck Swelling: Initial Presentation and Clinical Framing
sections.description: Introduces the patient’s subacute neck swelling and subtle systemic clues, and frames the diagnostic problem that initially mimicked deep neck infection and angioedema. Emphasizes the importance of targeted history and examination to detect inflammatory myopathy signals early.
subtopics: Case vignette highlights: 3-week progressive cervical swelling, proximal hip flexor weakness, mild myalgia; afebrile, stable vitals
Initial ED/ENT pathway: concern for Ludwig’s angina; CT neck showing diffuse strap muscle edema and retropharyngeal inflammation; nasendoscopy without obstructing lesions but increased secretions

Early differentials prompted by neck swelling: deep neck space infection, cellulitis/erysipelas, bacterial sialadenitis, idiopathic angioedema (histaminergic/bradykinin-mediated), superior vena cava syndrome

Atypical features for angioedema/infection: persistent non-tender swelling, absence of urticaria, triggers, family history, or ACE inhibitor use; normal temperature and oxygenation; subacute time course rather than abrupt onset

Subtle cutaneous/neuromuscular clues on exam: periungual erythema and nailfold microhemorrhages, rash over lateral thigh (Holster sign), reduced hip flexor power (4/5), generalized facial erythema including nasolabial folds

sections.section_title: From Mimic to Myositis: Diagnostic Workup and Reasoning
sections.description: Details the stepwise evaluation that shifted the working diagnosis from angioedema/infection to dermatomyositis, integrating laboratory tests, imaging, functional studies, autoantibody profiling, and biopsy findings.
subtopics: Laboratory triad suggesting myositis: markedly elevated CK (16,184 U/L), AST/ALT/LDH elevation; normal renal function and negative urine myoglobin
Angioedema exclusion workup: normal C4 and C1 esterase inhibitor level/function arguing against bradykinin-mediated angioedema
Autoimmunity screen: ANA 1:1280 speckled; extended myositis panel strongly positive for anti-SAE1; negative Mi-2, TIF1-γ, Jo-1, OJ

Imaging for distribution and severity of myositis: MRI thighs showing active myositis in hip girdle muscles; FDG-PET with diffuse abnormal uptake in head/neck, shoulder girdle, trunk, and pelvis muscles

Airway/swallowing involvement assessment: video fluoroscopic swallow showing severe pharyngeal dysphagia with penetration to vocal cords; PFTs with extrathoracic restrictive pattern consistent with upper airway/pharyngeal muscle weakness
Chest CT interpretation: non-cavitating pulmonary nodules and peribronchial consolidation consistent with aspiration pneumonitis; no fibrotic ILD
Gold-standard confirmation: muscle biopsy with perifascicular necrosis/degeneration/regeneration, perimysial inflammation, and capillary C5b-9 deposition typical of dermatomyositis

Malignancy screening per IMACS risk stratification: high-risk designation (dermatomyositis, dysphagia; intermediate factors: male sex, SAE1 positivity); CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET-CT, tumor markers, and planned upper/lower GI endoscopy

Differential refinement: distinguishing dermatomyositis from immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis, neuromuscular junction disorders (myasthenia gravis), drug/toxin-induced myopathy, and infection-related causes based on tempo, distribution, enzymes, antibodies, MRI/biopsy

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology Focus: Dermatomyositis, Anti-SAE1, and Pseudoangioedema
sections.description: Explains the disease mechanisms relevant to this case, the phenotype associated with SAE1 autoantibodies, and why dermatomyositis can masquerade as angioedema with prominent cervical edema and dysphagia.
subtopics: Dermatomyositis as complement-mediated microangiopathy: endothelial injury, capillary dropout, perifascicular ischemia leading to perifascicular atrophy/necrosis; C5b-9 deposition on endomysial capillaries
SAE1 autoantibodies: target the SUMO-activating enzyme complex; overview of sumoylation in transcriptional regulation and stress responses
SAE1-positive phenotype: prominent cutaneous disease (heliotrope, Gottron’s, shawl/V-sign), high rates of dysphagia and variable ILD; intermediate malignancy risk compared with other DM serotypes

Mechanism of ‘pseudoangioedema’: inflammatory myositis of cervical/strap muscles and subcutaneous tissue with capillary leak and lymphedema leading to non-histaminergic, non-bradykinin-mediated swelling
Dysphagia pathobiology: oropharyngeal and upper esophageal striated muscle weakness causing pooling, penetration/aspiration; explains extrathoracic restrictive PFTs and aspiration findings on CT
Biochemical patterns: CK and LDH from muscle injury; AST/ALT elevations reflecting myocyte, not hepatocyte, injury
Why angioedema tests are negative: normal C4/C1-INH in inflammatory myopathy-related edema; absence of pruritus/urticaria and slow evolution inconsistent with histaminergic events

sections.section_title: Management: Acute Stabilization and Disease Control
sections.description: Outlines evidence-informed treatment choices tailored to severe cervical myositis with dysphagia, including immunomodulation, airway and nutritional support, infection prophylaxis, and longitudinal monitoring.
subtopics: Acute immunosuppression for severe involvement: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days; transition to high-dose oral prednisone with slow taper guided by strength and CK
IVIG strategy: 2 g/kg loading over 5 days followed by monthly cycles; rationale in refractory dysphagia and severe myositis

Steroid-sparing therapy selection: mycophenolate mofetil (dose 1 g BID) chosen for tolerability and efficacy in DM; rationale for avoiding methotrexate (concerns re: ILD/fibrosis risk) and not using azathioprine/tacrolimus given response to MMF
B-cell depletion: rituximab (1 g ×2, 2 weeks apart) as add-on in severe disease or seropositive DM; expected time to response
Airway and swallow care: ENT monitoring, speech-language pathology-guided diet modification; nasogastric feeding for severe dysphagia; aspiration prevention

Infection screening and prophylaxis before/while immunosuppressed: viral hepatitis, HIV, TB evaluation; Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (TMP-SMX first-line; switch to nebulized pentamidine after hemolytic anemia)
Monitoring response and safety: serial CK and strength assessment, LFTs, CBC; pulmonary function tests; adjusting taper and IVIG intervals
Malignancy surveillance plan per IMACS risk: periodic symptom review, exams, labs, imaging; endoscopic evaluation for GI malignancy
Multidisciplinary coordination: immunology/rheumatology, ENT, neurology, pulmonology, speech therapy, dietetics

sections.description: Presents the patient’s clinical course and distills actionable lessons that prevent misdiagnosis and delays in care when dermatomyositis presents as neck swelling.
subtopics: Clinical course: rapid improvement of cervical edema and strength with therapy; CK normalization by 3 weeks; NG tube removed by 2 months; complete resolution of neck swelling by 3 months; prednisone discontinued by 7 months; stable respiratory function and near-complete resolution of aspiration changes on chest CT by 11 months

Key diagnostic pearls: order CK in unexplained, persistent neck swelling; examine for nailfold/periungual changes and subtle rashes (Holster sign); consider myositis antibodies when angioedema testing is non-diagnostic
Distinguishing features from true angioedema: subacute evolution, non-tender persistent edema, absence of urticaria/trigger, normal C4/C1-INH, concomitant proximal weakness or dysphagia
Role of biopsy and advanced imaging: muscle biopsy confirming DM pattern; MRI and FDG-PET for extent/severity mapping and to support inflammatory etiology
Management pitfalls to avoid: delays in immunosuppression while pursuing repeated infection workups; under-recognition of aspiration risk; premature steroid taper before objective improvement
Prognosis considerations in SAE1-positive DM: generally good response to combined immunomodulation; vigilance for ILD and malignancy despite reassuring initial screen

Practical algorithm (conceptual): persistent cervical edema without clear cause → check CK and examine skin/nails → myositis antibody panel/MRI if CK elevated or exam suggestive → secure airway/swallow assessment → initiate immunosuppression if DM likely → complete malignancy screening per risk profile
